title: WHY DID JESUS TELL MARY MAGDALENE NOT TO CLING TO HIM?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS TELL MARY MAGDALENE NOT TO CLING TO HIM?

She thought she had finally gotten Jesus back. But the risen Christ said something that has confused readers for centuries: “Do not cling to Me.” What happened in that garden was not rejection. It was resurrection teaching—and hidden inside His words is something every heart terrified of losing Jesus needs to hear.
There are moments when you have lost so much that, if God gave even one piece of it back, you would hold it so tightly your fingers would ache.
Mary Magdalene knew that feeling.
She had watched Jesus die.
Not metaphorically.
Not spiritually.
Die.
The voice that had spoken freedom into broken lives had gone silent.
The hands that touched lepers had been pierced.
The feet that walked dusty roads toward forgotten people had been nailed to wood.
The One Mary loved as Lord had been wrapped for burial and placed behind a stone.
Then Sunday came.
John tells us that Mary arrived at the tomb while it was still dark.
That detail almost feels like more than a description of the sky.
Because sometimes it is morning on the calendar while it is still midnight inside you.
Maybe you know something about that.
You still go to church.
Still whisper prayers.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
Still share Bible verses.
But somewhere underneath all of it, you are standing beside your own tomb asking why Jesus allowed something you loved to die.
Mary came looking for a corpse.
She was not expecting resurrection.
And perhaps that is the first scandal of grace in this story:
Jesus was already alive while Mary was still grieving as though everything was over.
Read that again.
The thing Mary believed was the ending had already been rewritten by God.
She just did not know it yet.
Peter and the other disciple came. They saw the empty tomb. They left.
Mary stayed.
Crying.
Then she looked inside and saw angels.
Even that did not stop her tears.
Then someone stood behind her.
She assumed He was the gardener.
Imagine the scene.
The risen Son of God is standing within speaking distance, and grief has made Him unrecognizable to her.
Jesus asks why she is weeping and whom she is seeking.
Mary, still believing someone has taken the body, essentially says: Tell me where you put Him, and I will take Him away.
Then Jesus says one word.
Her name.
“Mary.”
Everything changes.
She turns.
“Rabboni!”
Teacher.
Lord.
Jesus.
Alive.
The grave had lost.
Death had failed.
Rome had crucified Him, but Rome could not keep Him.
The stone had been sealed, but stones cannot imprison the Author of life.
Hell had thrown everything it had at the Son of God, and Sunday morning answered with an empty tomb.
Mary had come searching for Jesus among the dead.
Jesus found Mary among the living.
And then comes the sentence.
The strange sentence.
The sentence that can sound almost cold when removed from its context.
John 20:17 records the Greek:
“Μή μου ἅπτου, οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα…”
Mē mou haptou, oupō gar anabebēka pros ton patera…
Often rendered:
“Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.”
The older English “Touch Me not” can create the wrong picture.
Jesus was not acting as though Mary were dirty.
He was not suddenly untouchable.
He was not ashamed of her.
And He was certainly not rejecting the woman standing before Him.
The Greek verb translated “cling” is related to haptomai—ἅπτομαι—and here John uses ἅπτου (haptou).
The expression can carry the sense of holding onto, grasping, attaching oneself to, or clinging.
That matters.

Because later in the same chapter Jesus does not establish some universal rule that His resurrected body cannot be touched. When Thomas struggles to believe, Jesus directs him toward the evidence of His wounds.
So the issue in the garden is not simply physical contact.
Something deeper is happening.
Mary has found the Jesus she thought she had lost.
And naturally, desperately, beautifully, she wants to hold on.
Can you blame her?
If you watched someone you loved tortured and crucified on Friday and found Him standing alive before you on Sunday, would you want to let go?
Mary's reaction makes perfect human sense.
But Jesus is showing her that resurrection does not mean everything is simply returning to the way it was before Calvary.
He did not rise merely to resume the old arrangement.
The cross changed everything.
The resurrection announced something new.
The ascension was coming.
The Spirit would be given.
The Gospel would go outward.
And Mary could not remain forever in the garden clutching yesterday's experience of Jesus.
She had somewhere to go.
Someone to tell.
A message to carry.
Listen to the movement in Jesus' words:
“Do not cling to Me…”
then…
“Go…”
That may be one of the most important movements in Christian discipleship.
We encounter Christ…
and then Christ sends us.
Grace does not merely comfort us.
Grace commissions us.
The Gospel does not simply give us something beautiful to hold.
It gives us Someone glorious to proclaim.
Jesus continues:
“Go to My brothers…”
Do not race past those words.
“My brothers.”
Who were these “brothers”?
The disciples.
The same men who had scattered when Jesus was arrested.
Peter had denied Him.
Others had fled.
Their courage had collapsed when the pressure became unbearable.
And what does the resurrected Jesus call them?
Failures?
Cowards?
Disappointments?
Traitors?
No.
“My brothers.”
That is grace.
They failed Jesus.
Jesus did not stop being faithful to them.
Their worst night did not cancel His redemptive purpose.
The resurrection did not merely defeat death.
It announced that grace could still reach frightened disciples hiding behind locked doors.
Maybe that is where this story stops being Mary's story and becomes yours.
Because perhaps you love Jesus…
but you know you have failed Him.
Perhaps there are things in your history you wish you could erase.
Maybe you promised God you would never go back to that sin.
Then you went back.
Maybe you were on fire for Christ once.
Then something happened.
A disappointment.
A betrayal.
An unanswered prayer.
A secret compromise.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from God.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A season when prayer became rare, Scripture became distant, worship became mechanical, and conviction became easier to silence.
You still knew Christian language.
But your heart was drifting.
And perhaps somewhere inside you there is a fear you rarely admit:
“After everything I've done… does Jesus still want me?”
Look at Easter morning.
Look at the people Jesus calls “My brothers.”
Grace does not pretend their failure never happened.
Grace does something infinitely greater.
Jesus carries the judgment for sin at Calvary, rises victorious over death, and comes looking for sinners He intends to restore.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes the cross magnificent.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your rebellion.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin so seriously that the Son of God bears judgment, and loving sinners so deeply that the Son willingly gives Himself to save them.
That is why repentance matters.
Biblical grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you out of hiding.
Grace says you do not have to clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to receive you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Trust Christ.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop pretending the secret sin is harmless simply because nobody has discovered it.
Jesus did not walk out of a grave so you could spend your life decorating yours.
He came to make dead people live.
And maybe the hardest part of Mary’s encounter is this:
Sometimes loving Jesus means releasing the version of life you thought Jesus was supposed to give you.
Mary wanted Him there.
Jesus was preparing her for mission.
Mary wanted to hold.
Jesus told her to go.
Mary wanted the familiar.
Jesus was unfolding something larger than she could yet understand.
Have you ever prayed for God to restore something while God was teaching you to trust Him without it?
Have you ever begged Him to return life to the way it used to be?
“Jesus, give me that relationship back.”
“Give me that opportunity back.”
“Give me that person back.”
“Give me my old life back.”
“Give me the feeling I used to have when I prayed.”
Sometimes we are not clinging to Jesus.
We are clinging to the version of our story we expected Jesus to preserve.
There is a difference.
Mary had to learn that she could release her grip without losing her Savior.
So do we.
Because Christian faith is not possessing God on our terms.
It is belonging to Christ on His.
And the risen Jesus was not disappearing into irrelevance.
He was moving His redemptive mission toward its appointed fulfillment.
He tells Mary:
“I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God.”
Do you hear the intimacy?
Your Father.
Your God.
The woman who arrived believing everything had been taken from her walked away carrying news that would change human history.
She came grieving a dead Christ.
She left proclaiming a risen Christ.
John tells us what happened next:
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples,
“I have seen the Lord.”
Five words that changed everything.
She did not have every theological question answered.
She had encountered Jesus.
She had heard His voice.
And now she had a testimony.
“I have seen the Lord.”
That is what grace does.
It turns mourners into messengers.
It turns graves into testimonies.
It takes people whose stories look finished and puts resurrection language in their mouths.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your life has chapters you would never voluntarily read aloud.
Maybe there are pages stained with shame.
Divorce.
Sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Abortion.
Greed.
Unbelief.
Religious hypocrisy.
Broken promises.
Years wasted running from God.
Things done to you.
Things done by you.
Things nobody knows.
Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you wish had never been written.
The cross proves He knows exactly what sin costs.
The empty tomb proves sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
Your scandal does not become beautiful because sin was beautiful.
Your story becomes beautiful because grace entered the wreckage.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
By redeeming what the past could never repair.
And maybe today you are Mary standing in the garden.
Crying over something God has already begun transforming.
Maybe you are one of the disciples hiding behind a locked door because shame keeps telling you Jesus must be finished with you.
Maybe you are Thomas saying, “I need evidence.”
Maybe you are simply exhausted.
Still believing.
Still trying.
Still fighting battles nobody sees.
Hear the risen Christ.
The answer is not “try harder until you become worthy.”
The answer is Jesus.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Lord over death.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness.
Giving new life to those who trust Him.
And sending redeemed people into a broken world carrying good news.
Mary could not stay at the tomb.
Neither can we.
There are people who need to hear that Jesus still saves.
There are people on your Facebook friends list silently falling apart.
People posting jokes while fighting depression.
People posting family photographs while their marriage is bleeding behind closed doors.
People quoting Scripture while privately wondering whether God still hears them.
People who have not prayed sincerely in years.
People who think Christianity is merely religion because nobody has ever explained grace to them.
People convinced their past disqualifies them from coming home.
This is why sharing the Gospel matters.
Not because an algorithm deserves another post.
Because somebody behind a screen may be standing emotionally beside a tomb.
Not for applause.
For mission.
Send it privately to someone if tagging them publicly would embarrass them.
Be honest before God.
What are you still clinging to?
What are you afraid to surrender?
What hidden thing needs to come into Christ's light?
What disappointment have you allowed to become more authoritative than God's character?
What sin have you been excusing?
What grave have you mistaken for the ending?
Someone reading may desperately need proof that God still restores broken people.
But there is another way you can help this Gospel mission continue.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Christ-centered Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, and Gospel hope in front of people who desperately need it.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or a better standing before God.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption with His blood.
And Christian generosity must never be manipulated out of people through guilt or pressure.
Scripture teaches giving from the heart rather than under compulsion.
So pray first.
Take care of the responsibilities God has entrusted to you.
Support your local church and faithful Gospel work as you are convicted and able.
Think of it as voluntary ministry support—an offering of partnership, not a substitute we can biblically declare to be your required tithe.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep publishing.
Keep reaching.
Keep putting the name of Jesus into places where somebody may encounter the Gospel at the exact moment they were ready to give up.
And sharing costs nothing.
Pray.
Share.
One share can travel farther than you imagine.
One person you tag may return to Scripture.
One person you invite may hear the Gospel.
But merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
The Gospel is.
And then do what Mary did.
Go tell somebody.
Mary Magdalene walked into the garden thinking she had lost Jesus.
She walked out knowing death had lost Him.
And perhaps that is the word your heart needed today.
You do not need to hold Jesus tightly enough to keep Him alive.
He is risen.
You do not need to manufacture resurrection.
You need to trust the resurrected Christ.
You do not need to pretend your scandal never happened.
Bring it to the Savior whose wounds prove that grace was purchased at an unimaginable price.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Release what He is asking you to release.
Then rise from the place where you have been weeping…
and go.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Because the most astonishing thing about that garden was not that Mary finally found Jesus.
It was that the Jesus she thought she had lost already knew her name.
And when Christ calls your name, even the grave is no longer allowed to write your ending.
The hands Mary could not keep clinging to were the scarred hands already holding a future death could never steal.
